# Agentic coding with Claude {#sec-agentic}

An AI coding *agent* can read your files, run commands, look at the output, and iterate —
which makes it genuinely useful for the fiddly, cluster-specific work this book is about:
writing submit scripts, turning a loop into a job array, debugging an OOM kill, or making
sense of an unfamiliar codebase. This chapter is a practical guide to using one — Claude, in
particular — on MedicineBow, including where it helps, where it doesn't, and the two things
you must always do: **verify its output, and mind what data you send.**

## What "agentic" means

Older AI coding tools autocomplete the next line. An **agent** works at the level of a task:
you describe what you want, and it reads the relevant files, proposes changes, runs commands
(compile, test, submit a small job), reads the results, and adjusts — a loop, not a
single suggestion. That loop is what makes it fit HPC work, where the answer usually depends
on what a command *actually* prints (a `module spider`, a failed `sbatch`, a `seff` report),
not on what looks plausible in the abstract.

## Claude and Claude Code

**Claude** is Anthropic's family of models. The current ones are **Opus 4.8** (`claude-opus-4-8`)
and **Sonnet 5** (`claude-sonnet-5`) — Opus is the most capable for hard, multi-step work,
Sonnet is faster and cheaper for routine tasks — plus **Haiku 4.5** for the simplest, fastest
jobs and **Fable 5** (`claude-fable-5`) for the most demanding long-horizon work.

You reach Claude a few ways:

- **Claude Code** — Anthropic's coding agent. It runs in your terminal (and as a desktop app,
  in the browser at <https://claude.ai/code>, and as VS Code / JetBrains extensions), reads and
  edits files in your project, and runs commands. This is the one that fits cluster work.
- **The Claude API** — for building Claude into your own pipelines (e.g. an LLM step in a data
  workflow). Out of scope here, but worth knowing it exists.

## Using it with the cluster

Two workable setups:

1. **On your laptop, against a synced copy of your code.** Edit and iterate locally with the
   agent, then push or `rsync` (@sec-moving-data) to the cluster to run. Simplest, and keeps
   heavy work off shared machines entirely.
2. **On a login node.** Claude Code needs internet egress, which the login nodes have. The
   agent itself is lightweight, but remember the cardinal rule (@sec-cluster): **anything it
   runs, runs where you run it.** If you let it execute a real computation on the login node,
   that's the same violation as doing it yourself. Tell it to *submit jobs* and inspect
   results, not to run simulations in place — and do heavy interactive iteration inside an
   `salloc` session or a `debug`-partition job (@sec-interactive, @sec-queue-times).

::: {.callout-important}
## The agent doesn't know it's on a shared machine
It will happily run `python train.py` on the login node if you ask it to "run the training,"
because it can't see the etiquette you can. Be explicit: *"write and submit an sbatch job for
this; don't run it directly."* Treat the agent like a capable collaborator who has never used
a cluster before — which is exactly this book's audience.
:::

## What it's good for here

The cluster-specific tasks where an agent earns its keep:

- **Submit scripts.** "Write an sbatch script that runs `run.py` on one `mb` node with 8 cores
  and 16 GB, `fast` QOS, 2-hour limit." It knows the `#SBATCH` anatomy (@sec-anatomy); you
  check the account and the numbers.
- **Turning loops into job arrays.** Hand it a bash loop over 500 inputs and ask for an array
  version (@sec-arrays) — including the `sed -n`/0-index gotcha, which it will usually get
  right and you will verify.
- **Debugging failures.** Paste a `sacct` state and the `slurm-*.out` tail and ask *why*. It's
  good at recognizing OOM, timeouts, and "module not loaded in the script" (@sec-fail).
- **Checkpointing.** Adding save/resume and `--signal=B:USR1@120` handling to a long job
  (@sec-checkpointing).
- **Translating and explaining.** Converting a serial Python prototype to something that scales,
  reading an unfamiliar WRF or GDAL pipeline, or porting an analysis between Python, R, and
  Julia (@sec-hello-jobs).
- **Parsing cluster output.** One-off scripts to summarize `sacct` history, or to extract which
  array tasks failed.

## Verify everything it produces

This is the load-bearing rule. An agent is confident whether or not it's right, and it does
not know *your* cluster's specifics — the exact module versions, which partitions exist, what
your account may use. It will sometimes invent a plausible-but-wrong module name or flag.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check generated commands against the machine before you trust them
The module hierarchy is a common trap: an agent may write `module load gdal/3.13.0` after
`gcc/14.2.0`, which *fails* — that version needs `gcc/15.2.0` (@sec-modules). The fix is the
same habit the rest of this book preaches: run `module spider`, `sqos`, `showpartitions`,
`sacctmgr show assoc` and confirm. **Never submit an agent-written `sbatch` script, and never
run an agent-written `rm`/`mv`/`chmod`, without reading it first.** For destructive or
long/expensive jobs, test on the `debug` partition first (@sec-queue-times).
:::

A good workflow: let the agent draft, you read the diff, run it in a cheap `debug` job, and
only promote it to the real queue once it's known-good — exactly the edit-run-debug loop from
@sec-fail, with the agent doing the typing.

## Mind what data you send

Using Claude sends the code and any data you share to Anthropic's servers. For most
*code* — submit scripts, analysis, boilerplate — that's fine. Be careful with **data**:

- **Unpublished results, sensitive datasets, or anything export-controlled.** ARID touches
  power- and water-utility infrastructure; some of that may carry sharing restrictions. When in
  doubt, don't paste the data — share the *code* and describe the data's shape instead, and
  check your project's data-use policy and with your PI first.
- **Credentials.** Never paste API keys, passwords, or private SSH keys into a prompt. If you
  do by accident, rotate them (regenerate your SSH key via the portal, @sec-first-login).
- **Other people's data.** The `/project` filesystem is shared (@sec-storage); don't send a
  collaborator's data without their okay.

The rule of thumb: the agent is great at reasoning about *your code and the cluster*; keep
sensitive *inputs* out of it unless you've confirmed that's allowed.

## Getting access

Claude Code and the API are Anthropic products, separate from your ARCC account — see
<https://claude.ai/code> and <https://docs.claude.com> to get started. Usage is metered
(there are paid plans and API pricing); check whether your project or department already has
access before signing up individually. None of this runs through ARCC, so there's nothing to
request from `arcc-help@uwyo.edu` — but the code it helps you write still has to play by every
rule in this book.
